clue.text: Three-piece band's tenor moved to rear: he'll make you laugh

definitions.note: a clause describing a person, standing for the noun

indicators.note: a letter shifted to the back is taken out of its place and put at the end

blocks.note: a band of three players is a trio
T is the standard abbreviation for tenor

explanation.surface: A trio's tenor shuffles to the back of the stage and turns out to be the comic of the group.
explanation.walkthrough: TRIO loses its leading T, which is then added at the end, giving RIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a riot is informal praise for a person who is hilarious company.

clue.text: Communist severely criticises VIPs' treatment

blocks.note: red is the colour, and nickname, of communists
to carpet someone is to give them a dressing-down

explanation.surface: A communist pours scorn on the pampering given to the privileged.
explanation.walkthrough: To carpet someone is a British idiom for calling them in to be reprimanded.
explanation.definitionFit: Rolling out a red carpet is the ceremonial welcome given to celebrities and dignitaries.

clue.text: Managing some Adorno verse (Ein Gedicht)

indicators.note: only some of the following letters are wanted, a run lying inside the words

blocks.note: the run starts inside the philosopher's name and ends inside the German word for 'a'

explanation.surface: A reader at work on some lines by the German philosopher Adorno, with the German for 'a poem' added.
explanation.walkthrough: Ein Gedicht is German for 'a poem', which keeps the surface consistent; the letters run from adornO through VERSE and EIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Overseeing work means supervising and running it, the same as being in charge of it.

clue.text: Causing problems for English nationalist, audibly furious

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
N is a common abbreviation for nationalist
growling with rage, a fury you can hear

explanation.surface: An English nationalist making trouble while shouting angrily.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Audibly' is not a sound-alike signal here: it just turns 'furious' into a fury that makes a noise.
explanation.definitionFit: To ensnarl is to tangle up or entrap, so ensnarling something creates difficulties for it.

clue.text: LED seen flickering, causes annoyance

indicators.note: a flickering light is unsteady and jumps about, so the letters are disordered

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A flickering LED light is irritating to look at.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals of LED make it look like an abbreviation, but its three letters are simply part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle someone is to provoke or irritate them with persistent small jibes.

clue.text: Short month taken by Fitzgerald for short story

blocks.note: the calendar abbreviation of November
Ella Fitzgerald, the jazz singer

explanation.surface: Reads as F. Scott Fitzgerald spending a month writing a short story.
explanation.walkthrough: The literary context points to F. Scott Fitzgerald, but the wordplay wants the jazz singer Ella Fitzgerald's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A novella is a prose fiction longer than a typical short story but shorter than a novel.

clue.text: Expostulate and hold protest march? Leading Democrat ousted by Republican

indicators.note: whatever is leading comes at the front, so the first letter is meant
to be ousted by someone is to be thrown out and have them take your place

blocks.note: to stage a protest rally
the opening letter, which is the one swapped out
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A political tussle: protesters march while a Republican unseats a leading Democrat.
explanation.walkthrough: The D at the start of DEMONSTRATE is swapped for R.
explanation.definitionFit: To expostulate is to protest or argue earnestly against something, a close synonym.

clue.text: Greek character one thanks, getting round in

indicators.note: to get something is to take it on board, so one piece receives another

blocks.note: Roman numeral one
ta is British informal thanks
a round shape is the letter O, placed inside

explanation.surface: Someone thanking a Greek for getting a round of drinks in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting a round in' is British pub talk for buying the drinks, but here O goes in between I and TA.
explanation.definitionFit: Iota is the ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of our i.

clue.text: Primarily glamorous and lavish affair?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A description of a glitzy, extravagant party.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight it describes the event, and its initial letters spell it.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive social occasion, typically glamorous and lavish, held for celebration or fundraising.

clue.text: Ruminant finding grass in retreat

indicators.note: an army in retreat goes back the way it came

blocks.note: a reed is a tall waterside grass

explanation.surface: A grazing animal comes across grass while withdrawing to safety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' could be informer, but the reversal needs the plant REED.
explanation.definitionFit: Deer chew the cud, so they belong to the ruminants, like cattle, sheep and goats.

clue.text: Music with loud singer: Mercury?

blocks.note: first meaning: a loud, amplified style of rock
second meaning: a dense metallic element, the question mark flagging an example

explanation.surface: Seems to name Freddie Mercury of Queen as a loud rock singer.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercury looks like Freddie Mercury, but it is the element: dense metals such as mercury and lead are called heavy metals.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both a thunderous rock genre and dense toxic elements like lead, cadmium and mercury.

clue.text: Part of factory being refitted means bill? Yes

indicators.note: a refit strips something down and puts it back together in a fresh order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A factory manager confirms that the refit of part of the works means a big bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The question and answer break the fodder into odd chunks, but all twelve letters of 'means bill yes' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An assembly line is the sequence of workstations in a factory where products are put together.

clue.text: In 'less is more', wasting zero, displaying this?

definitions.text: In 'less is more', wasting zero, displaying this?

indicators.note: to waste something is to lose it, so a letter is dropped
a display lays things out in a new arrangement for show

blocks.note: taken as written
the motto taken as written
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Asks what trait is shown by someone who lives by 'less is more' and wastes nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: IN plus LESS IS MORE without its O is rearranged; read as a whole, the clue also describes the quality of a skinflint.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who wastes nothing and thinks less is more shows the stinginess of a miser.

clue.text: At 12, good to become King? That reeks!

definitions.note: an exclamation standing for the noun

indicators.note: one letter turning into another means it is swapped in place

blocks.note: a synonym of the solution to the clue numbered 12
G is the abbreviation for good, the letter replaced
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A twelve-year-old dreaming of being king while someone complains of a bad smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At 12' sounds like an age, but it points to 12-down, MISERLINESS, whose synonym STINGINESS has its G turned to K.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'that reeks!' complains of a foul odour, and stinkiness is the quality of smelling bad.

clue.text: Box in fights in S American port

indicators.note: one piece sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: a fray is a brawl or fight
a bento is a Japanese lunch box

explanation.surface: Boxing bouts staged in a South American harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Box' looks like a verb about fighting, but it is a noun: a bento is the Japanese packed-lunch box.
explanation.definitionFit: Fray Bentos is a port on the Uruguay River in Uruguay, also famous as a brand of meat pies.

clue.text: Strongly urges for drinks

definitions.note: a description of machines used to make drinks, standing for the noun

blocks.note: first meaning: pushes someone hard to do something
second meaning: machines that squeeze fruit to make wine or cider

explanation.surface: Someone insists on going for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For drinks' is a cryptic description: wine and cider are made in machines that crush the fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb meaning to urge insistently, and a noun for squeezing machines like the wine press or cider press.

clue.text: Alan's beginning to get increasingly wide. Nothing's consumed? That's increasingly wise

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter
something consumed is eaten up and gone, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
fatter, more stout
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: Alan is getting fatter; if he ate nothing he might be wiser.
explanation.walkthrough: STOUTER loses its O and follows A.
explanation.definitionFit: Astute means shrewd and perceptive, so the comparative form describes someone growing sharper of mind.

clue.text: Pet, a little tiny creepy-crawly? Odd

indicators.note: only a small bit of the word is wanted, its first letter

blocks.note: the opening letter
an ant is a small crawling insect
rum is British slang for strange

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a tiny insect would make a strange pet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pet' looks like a domestic animal, but it is the old British word for a sulk or fit of temper, as in 'in a pet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pet in the old sense is a fit of peevish ill humour, and a tantrum is an outburst of temper.

clue.text: Great musician's ear, most refined

indicators.note: refining something reworks it into a new, purer form

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A great musician's hearing is the most finely tuned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most refined' reads as a superlative, but 'most' joins 'ear' as fodder and 'refined' alone signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A maestro is a distinguished musician, especially a celebrated conductor or virtuoso performer.

clue.text: At repose, tucked into fold? For sure

indicators.note: something tucked into a thing is placed inside it

blocks.note: a ply is a layer or fold
having lain down, at rest

explanation.surface: Someone resting, tucked up in bed, sure of themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fold' could suggest a sheep pen, but here it means a layer, as in two-ply tissue.
explanation.definitionFit: Plainly and for sure both mean clearly, obviously, without any doubt.

clue.text: Constable, maybe one keeping boat secure

blocks.note: first meaning: an artist, such as John Constable
second meaning: a rope at a boat's bow used to tie it up

explanation.surface: A police constable on duty guarding a moored boat.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable looks like a police officer, but it is John Constable, the English landscape artist; 'maybe' flags him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an artist who works in oils and a mooring line attached to a small boat's bow.

clue.text: A square number, tripled: might you get help with this?

definitions.text: might you get help with this?

blocks.note: nine is three squared
two more copies of the number, making three in all

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle about squaring and tripling that ends by asking whether help is available.
explanation.walkthrough: 999 is the British emergency telephone number, the equivalent of 911 in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Dialling 999 in Britain summons the emergency services: police, fire brigade or ambulance.

clue.text: Chills dry drop of Italian when laid up

indicators.note: a drop is a tiny amount, here a single first letter
in a down clue, something laid upward is read bottom to top

blocks.note: sec is the wine term for dry
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone chilling a dry Italian wine while ill in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Laid up sounds like being bedridden, but in a down clue it signals reading upward.
explanation.definitionFit: To ice something is to cool it, so chills and ices are matching verbs.

clue.text: Stuck in hesitant utterance, Everyman's held up monarch?

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising something up flips its order
something stuck in a thing is lodged inside it

blocks.note: er is the sound of hesitation
the setter speaking of himself: Everyman is, I'm

explanation.surface: The setter, stammering, confesses to being delayed by a king.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter often refers to himself by his pen name, so 'Everyman's' is 'I'm'. The question mark admits an emir is not always strictly a monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: An emir is a Muslim ruler or prince, sovereign over an emirate in the Arab world.

clue.text: According to Spooner, Jones 'n' Winslet describe the game

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words

blocks.note: singer Tom Jones and actress Kate Winslet, first names joined; swap the opening sounds

explanation.surface: Two celebrities, Tom Jones and Kate Winslet, providing commentary on a match.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom Jones is a Welsh singer and Kate Winslet an English actress; swapping T and K gives 'Kom 'n' Tate'.
explanation.definitionFit: To commentate is to give a running description of a sporting event as it happens.

clue.text: Money's in the post, did you say?

indicators.note: asking what was said points to the sound rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a letter in the post has been dispatched

explanation.surface: The familiar excuse that the payment has already been mailed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The cheque's in the post' is a stock excuse for late payment; 'in the post' means sent.
explanation.definitionFit: A cent is a coin, one hundredth of a dollar or euro, so a small sum of money.

clue.text: Regurgitated roast grubs in French city

indicators.note: regurgitated food comes back up in a mess, its parts thrown around

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A queasy traveller bringing up a meal of roasted grubs while in France.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of 'roast grubs' are reordered.
explanation.definitionFit: Strasbourg is a city in Alsace, eastern France, home to the European Parliament.

clue.text: Employs house-sitter? Not entirely

indicators.note: only part of the words is taken, a run inside them

blocks.note: the run straddles the hyphen

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether a homeowner hires a house-sitter, only partly.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run from inside 'house' across the hyphen into 'sitter'.
explanation.definitionFit: To employ a tool or method is to use it, so the two verbs are synonyms.
